Intrinsic Core is interoperable with ROS via standard workspaces, message definitions, and tools, allowing developers to combine their existing ROS packages with Intrinsic capabilities. items.title: Data collection framework update to Lyrical, Jazzy and Rolling
items.summary: Hi ROS2 community! 3 years and ~150 commits since my last announcement , my open-source data collection project for ros2 is now able to run on lyrical, jazzy and rolling. DC runs on the robot. It collects measurements, validates every record against a JSON schema, and ships them to your own PostgreSQL or object storage. It was already released some years ago and here is what changed since recently: Jazzy, Lyrical and Rolling are now three maintained distros, each with its own container images on ghcr. A new uploader moves maps, camera frames and videos to object storage over verified, resumable transfers. Every file’s metadata becomes a queryable record. Deployment files ship for Compose, Quadlet and Kubernetes, and the docs are versioned per distro. To do all of this, I had to drop Fluent bit support and use Vector instead. Integration became much easier. What about Foxglove for example? It is a full data platform: live visualization, teleop, recording, searchable replay, collaboration. DC is narrower. items.articleText: [GSoC 2026] Scalable Multi-Robot Simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo - Projects - Open Robotics Discourse [GSoC 2026] Scalable Multi-Robot Simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo Projects ros2 , gazebo C88-YQ November 2, 2026, 4:19pm 1 Organization: Open Robotics Contributor: Jiayi Cai (@C88-YQ ) Mentor: Addisu Taddese (@azeey ) Community Meeting Talk : Talk video ; Talk slides Project Overview Multi-robot simulation is widely used in robotics research and development, including warehouse automation, robot swarms, and multi-robot coordination. However, setting up a multi-robot simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo can require a lot of repetitive configuration. There are two main challenges: Communication isolation: When multiple robots share the same SDF model, they may also share the same topic and service names, leading to conflicts. Users often need to create separate SDF files or use templates to configure different names for each robot. ROS-Gazebo bridge configuration: Each robot usually requires several topic and service bridges. As the number of robots increases, manually maintaining these configurations becomes more difficult. The goal of this GSoC project was to simplify multi-robot simulation by introducing two main features: Model namespace support: Allow multiple robots to share the same SDF model while keeping their communication interfaces separate. Automated ROS-Gazebo bridging: Automatically discover and create bridges for matching ROS 2 and Gazebo topics and services, reducing manual configuration. These features aim to make multi-robot simulations easier to set up, maintain, and scale. Main Work 1. Model Namespace Support The first major part of the project was introducing model namespace support across SDFormat, Gazebo Sim, and ROS-Gazebo integration. With this feature, users can assign a namespace to a model, allowing supported Gazebo plugins to use it when resolving topic and service names. Model namespace support 1212×602 191 KB Namespaces can be configured directly in SDF files using the <model> namespace attribute or the <include> namespace element. They can also be specified when spawning models at runtime. For nested models, namespaces are resolved by searching from the current model up through its parents, combining relative namespaces until an absolute namespace is found. The resolved namespace is then used as a prefix for default and relative topic and service names, while absolute names remain unchanged. Backward compatibility is preserved, so models without a namespace continue to use their existing topic and service naming behavior. This feature provides a consistent approach for handling topic and service names across Gazebo plugins. It also allows multiple robots to share the same SDF model while keeping their communication interfaces separate, making multi-robot simulations much easier to set up and maintain. Namespace support has been added to DiffDrive and extended to other drive plugins and sensors, with several PRs still under review. 2. Automated ROS-Gazebo Bridge Previously, users needed to manually configure the names, message types, and communication directions of their bridges. This becomes repetitive when working with many robots that have similar communication interfaces. The new automated bridge can discover matching topics and services on the ROS 2 and Gazebo sides and create the corresponding bridges. As illustrated below, the process consists of three main steps: discovering available interfaces, matching them based on their names and compatible message types, and creating the required bridges. Automated birdge 1744×400 254 KB The feature is optional and can be enabled using the automated_bridge.enable parameter. It also provides two optional configuration parameters: include_patterns : Select which topics and services should be considered. exclude_patterns : Exclude specific topics and services from automated bridging. For example, the following configuration enables automated bridging for interfaces under /robot1 while excluding camera-related topics: # example ros_gz_bridge: ros__parameters: automated_bridge: enable: true include_patterns: - "/robot1.*" exclude_patterns: - ".*camera.*" The automated bridge continuously checks for new interfaces, allowing it to discover topics and services created after the simulation starts. It also supports using manual and automated bridge configurations together. Within the same bridge instance, manually configured bridges take priority, and automated bridging handles the remaining interfaces. To evaluate the overhead of continuous discovery and matching, I tested the automated bridge with a simulation containing 12 robots, 124 Gazebo topics, and 94 Gazebo services, along with a separate ROS 2 node providing 115 topics and 44 services. With actual bridge creation disabled during this test, average CPU usage increased from 2.44% to 3.32% , while memory usage remained nearly unchanged. This suggests that the discovery and matching process adds relatively little overhead in the tested setup. 3. Documentation and Demos Three documentation updates and two demos were prepared to demonstrate the new features and help users get started. Documentation: Model Namespace — How to configure and use model namespaces. Automated Bridge — How to enable and configure automated bridging. Multi-Robot Tutorial — How to use both features together in multi-robot simulations. Demos: Multi-Robot Demo — Demonstrates model namespaces and automated bridging with multiple robots. Warehouse Demo — Demonstrates independent control of four Mecanum-wheel robots sharing the same SDF model. Project Status and Pull Requests The project involved changes across several repositories, including sdformat , gz-msgs , gz-sim , gz-transport , ros_gz , and Gazebo documentation. As of 1st November 2026, the core namespace infrastructure and several related features have been merged, while some plugin integrations, automated bridging, demos, and documentation are still under review. Under review Future Work 1. Extending Namespace Support Namespace support will continue to be extended to the remaining Gazebo plugins and sensors. Some PRs are already under review, and additional issues have been prepared for community contributors. 2. Handling TF Frame IDs Although namespaces can separate TF topics for different robots, the frame IDs inside TF messages may still conflict. Two possible approaches are to maintain independent TF trees for each robot or rewrite frame IDs on the ROS 2 side before combining them. Future work will explore supporting namespace-based frame ID prefixes directly in Gazebo. 3. Further Improvements to Automated Bridging The discovery and direction inference logic developed for automated bridging could also be used to simplify manual bridge configuration, reducing the need to specify message types and bridge directions manually. items.title: Speeding up planning decisions with AI
items.summary: Google DeepMind and UK government work together to reduce planning assessment times
items.articleText: October 31, 2026 Responsibility & Safety Speeding up planning decisions with AI Owen Larter and David Thacker Share PlanAssist has shown it can cut the time planning officers spend assessing householder applications by up to 58%. PlanAssist - an AI planning tool that handles the heavy lifting of routine applications so officers can focus their expertise where it matters most - is to be made available to an additional 12 local planning authorities across England. In early pilot testing across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset, PlanAssist showed it could bring the average time a planning officer spent on householder assessment tasks down by 58%. Designed to support human judgement, the tool speeds up routine checks while ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every application. Planning bottlenecks have real costs. For the economy, they slow progress toward the UK government's goal of building 1.5 million new homes by 2029. For families, that can mean months of waiting on approval for something as simple as a loft conversion, conservatory, or extension. Built with Gemini, PlanAssist is part of Google DeepMind’s broader partnership with the UK government to explore how AI can help transform planning and other public services. How PlanAssist supports officers Routine householder applications account for up to 70% of planning officers’ workloads. They're often simple to approve but take up a disproportionate share of their time. Developed by Google DeepMind in collaboration with the UK government, Google Cloud, and Faculty, PlanAssist streamlines this work, giving planning officers automated support with processing applications and drafting assessment recommendations. First, it validates application documents and architectural drawings, checking that the required information has been submitted so the application can proceed. Next, it checks the application against heritage constraints (such as tree preservation orders), and local and national planning policies. It also checks whether any issues or objections have previously been raised, such as by local residents. Finally, it drafts fully cited reports that can be edited by planning officers before they reach a final decision. Since June, the tool has been piloted across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset councils, and has shown encouraging early results. In addition to more than halving the officer assessment time per application, more than 70% of the reports generated by the tool - including things like whether an application complies with local planning rules, or whether the applicant has submitted all required documentation - were approved by officers with no edits required. Your browser does not support the video tag. See how Plan Assist works. Moving from pilot to scale PlanAssist is now moving into a 12-month Beta phase using live applications, starting with a subset of councils. Twelve more councils will be onboarded in three cohorts, bringing the total involved to 15. Together, these councils include metropolitan and rural districts across the country, allowing us to test PlanAssist’s capabilities across a diverse range of communities. Subject to successful testing, the government plans for the tool to be made available to all councils in England in 2027, with every assessment reviewed and approved by a qualified planning officer before any decision is made. AI in service of communities Planning decisions shape everyday lives, from a family adding a nursery to a homeowner preparing for winter. By handling time-consuming administrative tasks, and ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every decision, PlanAssist shows how AI can help cut backlogs and approve applications faster. Providing access to these new councils is the natural next step, and we look forward to continuing to support the UK government as they seek to build more homes and unlock economic growth across the country. Try it for free The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence” 2nd November 2026 I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. First, the updated chart Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: Here’s a link to the larger image . For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”. Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, available from here . Here’s a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses—here’s my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. The changing language of the questions As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn’t find it. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.) The BTOS about page explains what happened: Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434 . The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording—the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday. Is this going to affect the survey? The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results. The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn’t going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out “formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI”. I can’t help but laugh at the absurdity of “SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service” though. items.articleText: Perspective The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026 Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) Republish Share Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies. That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut. The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is. Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer. Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due. The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models. Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so. Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments. Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic. Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins AI industry margins Demand pressure: Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI. Commoditization: Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices. Cost pressures: High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash. External constraints: Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation. Source: Matthew U. Scherer and Maya Jenkins, “Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts,” Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, October 2026 (Figure 13, p. 30).Interactive graphic: Tech Policy Press First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%). Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid . Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list. Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential. In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required. That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion , and the prices for some components are soaring. That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments. And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task. Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher. Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost. If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash ; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice. It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect .” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches. The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy. items.title: Churchill Capital XI shareholders approve $2.5B Agility Robotics humanoid SPAC
items.summary: Deal is expected to provide approximately $465 million in gross capital as Agility expands deployments of its Digit humanoid with industrial customers. The post Churchill Capital XI shareholders approve $2.5B Agility Robotics humanoid SPAC appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics Agility Robotics has cleared a major hurdle in its planned initial public offering (IPO). Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the special purpose acquisition company’s (SPAC) proposed business combination with the humanoid developer, moving Agility closer to becoming a publicly-traded company. More than 84% of votes cast at a special shareholder meeting on Nov. 2 supported the deal. The SPAC is expected to close on Nov. 4. The combined company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker symbol AGLT. Churchill Capital stock finished up nearly 14% on Nov. 2. The transaction is expected to provide Agility with approximately $465 million in gross capital before expenses. That funding will support commercial expansion, customer deployments and manufacturing capacity as the company looks to scale its Digit humanoid robot business. The revised capital figure reflects a reduction from the more than $620 million in gross proceeds anticipated when the merger was announced in June. Following the expiration of Churchill XI’s shareholder redemption deadline, the companies now expect approximately $164 million from Churchill’s trust account, approximately $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) financing led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity funding Agility received following the initial SPAC announcement. The original transaction valued Agility at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value. Existing Agility shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company rather than receive cash in the transaction. Agility is entering the public markets with more than a proposed product roadmap. Its Digit robots are already operating in 9 customer environments, with logistics and manufacturing emerging as the company’s primary commercial markets. One of its most established relationships is with GXO Logistics. The companies began working together in 2023 and signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service agreement in 2024 to deploy Digit at GXO’s facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. There, Digit has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors. In October, the companies announced an expansion to two additional GXO facilities: Statesville, N.C., and Lebanon, Tenn. Digit will initially support repetitive material-handling tasks in e-commerce fulfillment operations. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 using Digit 4, with plans to transition to the newer Digit 5 as it becomes commercially available. Agility is also moving into manufacturing. In October, agricultural equipment maker AGCO signed a commercial agreement to pilot Digit at its Hesston , Kan., production facility beginning in 2027. Initial tasks will include sorting and stacking parts and placing totes for storage. Submit your innovation now! Agility has previously claimed it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5 , its next-generation humanoid unveiled in September. The company says early access for customers is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of that year. That order figure is an important indicator of customer interest, but it should not be confused with current revenue. The multi-year value is expected to be realized over time and remains subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Agility’s RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Ore., is designed for annual production capacity of up to 10,000 robots. The company is also expanding its software, deployment and service capabilities, including through its Agility Arc fleet-management platform. items.title: Tutor Intelligence raises Series B to scale model training, robot deployments
items.summary: Tutor Intelligence has raised funding to further develop its picking robots, networked intelligence, and commercial deployments. The post Tutor Intelligence raises Series B to scale model training, robot deployments appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Tutor trains its Sonny robot on real-world manipulation tasks. Credit: Eugene Demaitre Real-world data, human “tutors,” and simulation are all part of the recipe for training AI models to enable next-generation robots to tackle a widening variety of tasks. Tutor Intelligence Inc. today said it has raised $75 million in Series B funding as it works toward general-purpose robotics. “It’s not only that Tutor’s models let robots do jobs that robots have never been able to do before,” stated Josh Gruenstein, co-founder and CEO of Tutor Intelligence. “This type of intelligence also makes robots affordable on a whole new level. We’re unlocking much broader access to the solutions that businesses need to survive and that make basic goods cheaper for everybody. And the demand is there. We can hardly build robots fast enough.” Tutor Intelligence spun out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (MIT CSAIL ) in 2021. The Watertown, Mass.-based company asserted that it is building a full technology stack to “close the gap between what robots can do and what people can do.” Data flywheel accelerates robot deployment “Artificial intelligence has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images,” said Tutor Intelligence. “The physical world has no such record to train on, and AI has yet to transform it in the same way.” The company has deployed fleets of internet-connected robots into production environments, where they do real work for customers with input from remote operators known as “tutors.” It uses the real-world data to train better frontier models, ultimately making the robots more capable. Tutor claimed that its “full-stack platform” and “data flywheel” accelerate deployment, making robots more scalable, safer, and more affordable. Instead of a robots-as-a-service (RaaS ) model, business pay Tutor by the hour or by the pick, the same way they pay for manual labor. Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, added Tutor. The company said it handles deployment and maintenance and regularly sends software and intelligence upgrades. Tutor said its approach is bringing automation to tasks that have long defied conventional, deterministic robotics. It opened a “Data Factory ” earlier this year to evaluate policies across 100 physical robots. Submit your innovation now! Tutor Intelligence gets traction with Sonny and Cassie Tutor’s Data Factory includes the Sonny two-armed, semi-humanoid robots for each picking. Cassie is a mobile manipulator designed for case picking and palletizing . The company reported that twice as many of its robots are working in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago. It said it is on track to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027, all of which will be built in and deployed from the U.S. (The tutors may be overseas.) The robots are currently moving, lifting, and manipulating objects across some of the country’s largest manufacturing and logistics networks. They handle breakfast cereals, snacks, candy, cosmetics, home goods, toys, and more. Tutor noted that its growth reflects maturing enterprise adoption of physical AI, as companies move from pilots to expectations of a return on investment from automating their operations. Nearly a third of organizations that received Tutor robots in the past 12 months were existing customers installing more robots, it said. Funding to support more training and manufacturing Andreessen Horowitz led Tutor Intelligence’s Series B round, which brings its total capital raised to $117 million. Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led the company’s Series A and seed rounds, respectively, also participated. “Tutor’s insight is that deployment isn’t just the destination for robotics research—it’s how you overcome its limitations,” said Raghu Raghuram, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz and former CEO of VMware. “Rather than asking the real world to fit the research, Tutor starts with what real-world deployments demand and works backward through distribution, hardware and research,” he added . “Continual learning across an expanding range of deployments is the path from specialized capabilities to general-purpose robotics.” Tutor said its latest investment its frontier robot foundation model training, as well as manufacturing and deployment of Sonny and Cassie. It announced the latest models of its robots and underlying platform last month. Tell Us What You Think! Cancel reply This site uses Akismet to reduce spam. Learn how your comment data is processed. items.title: Gentherm designs ThermAffyx to protect, move patients during robotic surgeries
items.summary: ThermAffyx addresses secure positioning and heating of patients for robot-assisted surgical procedures with a minimal OR footprint. The post Gentherm designs ThermAffyx to protect, move patients during robotic surgeries appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: ThermAffyx both securely positions and warms patients during robot-assisted surgeries. Source: Gentherm Many healthcare advances come from within that industry, but innovations from other industries can also find a role. Gentherm Medical has designed its ThermAffyx Patient Safety System based on thermal management experience from the automotive industry. The system both securely positions a patient and provides patient warming for robot-assisted surgery . Gentherm Inc. said ThermAffyx does both while minimizing the amount of space required and without the need for forced-air equipment. The Novi, Mich.-based company launched the system at the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) Global Surgical Conference this year. Gentherm noted that numerous medical professionals told it that “almost all of their robotics patients are hypothermic.” Adam Hauke, global director for product strategy and innovation at Gentherm, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report . Gentherm addresses Trendelenburg challenge What is the challenge that ThermAffyx addresses, and how are patient positioning and hypothermia handled conventionally? Hauke: The ThermAffyx Patient Safety System combines active patient warming and secure positioning into a single solution, helping address two critical perioperative challenges: maintaining normothermia and reducing patient movement during surgery. The current standard of care consists of forced-air warming solutions and a securement pad. Historically, warming and positioning have been addressed independently because, in many surgical procedures, they do not significantly interfere with one another. However, that’s not the case in most robotic-assisted surgeries. These procedures frequently require patients to remain in Trendelenburg positioning, where the body is tilted head-down to provide surgical access to the pelvis and lower abdomen. Patients may remain in these positions for extended periods while robotic systems are docked and utilized. This positioning introduces several challenges, including increased pressure and shear forces that can contribute to pressure injuries, the potential for nerve-related complications if positioning is not optimized, and the risk of patient movement or shifting during lengthy procedures. Underbody securement pads are designed to address these positioning challenges. At the same time, maintaining normothermia becomes more challenging because robotic equipment occupies the physical space that traditional over-body warming solutions must be deployed in. In these situations, clinicians often rely on under-body warming approaches, but they are difficult or impossible to use in robotics because they would interfere with the underbody securement pads used for safely positioning the patient. Suddenly, warming and positioning are no longer separate considerations. They are competing for the same real estate. How much do patients move around during surgical procedures? Hauke: In the routine course of things in the operating room, “patient movement” is not tracked. “Patient movement,” if it is recorded it is done so as “light anesthesia.” It is usually referring to if the patient’s anesthetic wears off prematurely and they move a hand or leg type thing. No one is measuring anything on the OR table related to patient movement, as everything is under the sterile drape at that point. The only way the surgical team knows if a patient moves, is if there is tension on the robotic instruments typically. Any unintended patient movement during robot-assisted surgeries can vary greatly based on a number of factors. There are multiple contributing individual factors such as patient weight, height, and body proportions, as well as procedure-based factors such as the patient position, the steepness the OR table is tilted to and whether or not other positioning solutions are used such as stirrups. If there is a shift related to Trendelenburg, it’s usually noticed by anesthesia as difficult respirations or a drop in capnography. An actual measurable shift in a patient on the OR table doesn’t occur very often and is not currently a recorded stat. Submit your innovation now! Is there a weight or size range for the system? Hauke: The ThermAffyx System is intended for adult patients and has been tested on individuals up to 297 lb. [134.7 kg]. The Pad is designed so that a patient can be positioned anywhere within the heating zone to receive active warming. The Pad’s safety sensors do not require direct patient contact to function. As always, clinicians should follow their facility’s protocols and guidelines for safe patient positioning. Does Gentherm’s system require more power than existing setups? Hauke: No, ThermAffyx runs on standard hospital electrical outlets. Is there any danger of thermal or electromagnetic interference with certain surgical instruments? Hauke: We have mitigated the risks of compatibility with other devices as far as possible. The system has been designed and verified to comply with all applicable industry standards and FDA guidance — including compatibility with electrocautery, diathermy, defibrillation equipment, RFID devices, wireless power transfer devices, and 5G cellular networks. Therefore, the risk of thermal or EM interference is low. However, there is always residual risk of issues occurring. We do not control the design and use of external devices that may be used in combination with ThermAffyx, and thus cannot guarantee other devices have been designed to meet the same standards or that devices are being used per the manufacturer’s labeling. ThermAffyx moves toward the market How is the system progressing toward commercialization? Hauke: Commercialization is well under way. Our teams are in active trials across the country with strong adoption in both new accounts and our legacy Gentherm accounts. How difficult was it to get U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance? Hauke: Although Gentherm is an expert in patient warming devices, gaining FDA clearance for ThermAffyx took careful development planning and execution. This is the first and only all-in-one product to have Class II indications for use for maintaining normothermia and securement. To ensure the proper steps were being taken, we started the process with a Q-Sub to the FDA to receive their feedback on our claims and validation plan. We then implemented the appropriate design and testing per the FDA feedback to validate our claims. An additional requirement with the FDA is to prove the usability of your device. The operation of the device must fit flawlessly into clinicians’ regular workflows to ensure the system can be used safely without introducing complexity. Nurses and anesthesiologists provided critical inputs to the design through focus groups, then validated the design in extensive hands-on usability studies. Does this add to the cost of OR equipment or surgical procedures? Hauke: While ThermAffyx does add incremental cost for the technology — lower than most capital budget thresholds — the more important consideration is its potential impact on reducing costly downstream complications. By helping to reduce the risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia, patient movement or pressure related injuries, the system may help avoid adverse events that can increase length of stay, require additional treatment, and drive higher overall costs of care. In robotic surgery, these procedures are already supported by established reimbursement structures and procedure codes, making this technology a natural fit within the existing surgical workflow. Will you be selling it directly or through third parties? Hauke: ThermAffyx is available for purchase through Gentherm’s U.S. contract sales team. Are there other potential use cases for ThermAffyx and its component technologies? Hauke: ThermAffyx was specifically designed to address the challenge of maintaining normothermia in patients undergoing minimally invasive and robotic-assisted procedures, particularly in gynecological, urological, or general surgery cases that require patient positioning in tilt. However, its innovative 3-in-1 design offers benefits that extend well beyond these initial applications. By integrating warming technology into a pressure redistributing underbody foam pad, ThermAffyx can help support patient temperature management in a wide range of surgical settings where maintaining normothermia can be difficult including orthopedics, cardiovascular, colorectal, and plastics cases. About The Author Eugene Demaitre Eugene Demaitre is editorial director of the robotics group at Arrowfly (previously WTWH Media). He was senior editor of The Robot Report from 2019 to 2020 and editorial director of Robotics 24/7 from 2020 to 2023. Prior to working at Arrowfly, Demaitre was an editor at BNA (now part of Bloomberg), Computerworld, TechTarget, and Robotics Business Review. Demaitre has participated in robotics webcasts, podcasts, and conferences worldwide. He has a master's from the George Washington University and lives in the Boston area. Tell Us What You Think! entries.title: Intrinsic Core 오픈소스 공개: ROS 호환 실시간 제어 및 모션 플래닝 프레임워크
entries.reason: 제조 워크셀 구축을 위해 하드웨어 비종속적 실시간 제어와 ROS 상호 운용성을 지원하는 오픈소스 런타임을 제공함

facts.statement: Intrinsic은 제조 현장 배치에 사용해 온 기본 기능과 서비스를 오픈소스화한 Intrinsic Core를 공개했으며, 표준 워크스페이스와 메시지 정의를 통해 ROS와 상호 운용된다.
facts.quote: Intrinsic Core is interoperable with ROS via standard workspaces, message definitions, and tools

entries.title: ROS 2 데이터 수집 프레임워크 DC, Lyrical·Jazzy·Rolling 지원 업데이트
entries.reason: ROS 2 로봇 데이터 수집 시 검증된 스키마 기반 전송 파이프라인과 Vector 기반 경량 배포 환경을 제공함

facts.statement: ROS 2 데이터 수집 프로젝트 DC가 Lyrical, Jazzy, Rolling 배포판을 지원하도록 업데이트되었으며, Fluent Bit 대신 Vector를 도입하고 측정값을 JSON 스키마로 검증해 PostgreSQL 또는 객체 스토리지로 전송한다.
facts.quote: runs on the robot. It collects measurements, validates every record against a JSON schema, and ships them to your own PostgreSQL

entries.title: GSoC 2026: ROS 2와 Gazebo 기반 확장 가능한 다중 로봇 시뮬레이션 개발
entries.reason: 다중 로봇 시뮬레이션 구성 시 SDF 모델 재사용을 위한 네임스페이스와 자동 브리지 기능의 구현 현황 및 사용법을 안내함

facts.statement: GSoC 2026 프로젝트를 통해 여러 로봇이 통신 인터페이스를 분리하면서 동일한 SDF 모델을 공유할 수 있는 모델 네임스페이스 지원과 ROS 2-Gazebo 자동 브리지 기능이 개발되었다.
facts.quote: Allow multiple robots to share the same SDF model while keeping their communication interfaces separate.

entries.title: OpenAI, 대규모 Codex 개발 지원을 위한 Git 호환 백엔드 Pando 소개 (제목 기반)
entries.reason: AI 코딩 모델 환경에서 대규모 Git 작업을 처리하기 위해 설계된 전용 백엔드 아키텍처 사례를 다룸

facts.statement: OpenAI는 Codex가 가능하게 한 개발 규모에 맞춰 설계된 Git 호환 백엔드인 Pando를 구축했다고 밝혔다 (제목 기반).
facts.quote: Git-compatible backend designed for the scale of development that Codex makes possible.

entries.title: Google DeepMind와 영국 정부, AI 기반 인허가 계획 도구 PlanAssist 파일럿 확대
entries.reason: 공공 인허가 행정 업무에서 생성형 AI 기반 자동화 검증 도구 도입 현황과 처리 시간 단축 효과를 제시함

facts.statement: Google DeepMind와 영국 정부는 주택 소유자 인허가 신청서 검토 시간을 최대 58% 단축한 Gemini 기반 AI 계획 도구 PlanAssist를 잉글랜드 내 12개 추가 지자체로 확대 적용한다.

entries.title: LLM CLI 도구 0.37 릴리스: gpt-6.1 모델 추가 및 멀티모달 임베딩 지원
entries.reason: 커맨드라인에서 신규 LLM 모델 호출 및 다양한 바이너리 타입을 지원하는 임베딩 처리 개선 사항을 안내함

selectedItems.title: Data collection framework update to Lyrical, Jazzy and Rolling
selectedItems.summary: Hi ROS2 community! 3 years and ~150 commits since my last announcement , my open-source data collection project for ros2 is now able to run on lyrical, jazzy and rolling. DC runs on the robot. It collects measurements, validates every record against a JSON schema, and ships them to your own PostgreSQL or object storage. It was already released some years ago and here is what changed since recently: Jazzy, Lyrical and Rolling are now three maintained distros, each with its own container images on ghcr. A new uploader moves maps, camera frames and videos to object storage over verified, resumable transfers. Every file’s metadata becomes a queryable record. Deployment files ship for Compose, Quadlet and Kubernetes, and the docs are versioned per distro. To do all of this, I had to drop Fluent bit support and use Vector instead. Integration became much easier. What about Foxglove for example? It is a full data platform: live visualization, teleop, recording, searchable replay, collaboration. DC is narrower. However, setting up a multi-robot simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo can require a lot of repetitive configuration. There are two main challenges: Communication isolation: When multiple robots share the same SDF model, they may also share the same topic and service names, leading to conflicts. Users often need to create separate SDF files or use templates to configure different names for each robot. ROS-Gazebo bridge configuration: Each robot usually requires several topic and service bridges. As the number of robots increases, manually maintaining these configurations becomes more difficult. The goal of this GSoC project was to simplify multi-robot simulation by introducing two main features: Model namespace support: Allow multiple robots to share the same SDF model while keeping their communication interfaces separate. Automated ROS-Gazebo bridging: Automatically discover and create bridges for matching ROS 2 and Gazebo topics and services, reducing manual configuration. These features aim to make multi-robot simulations easier to set up, maintain, and scale. Main Work 1. Model Namespace Support The first major part of the project was introducing model namespace support across SDFormat, Gazebo Sim, and ROS-Gazebo integration. With this feature, users can assign a namespace to a model, allowing supported Gazebo plugins to use it when resolving topic and service names. Model namespace support 1212×602 191 KB Namespaces can be configured directly in SDF files using the <model> namespace attribute or the <include> namespace element. They can also be specified when spawning models at runtime. For nested models, namespaces are resolved by searching from the current model up through its parents, combining relative namespaces until an absolute namespace is found. The resolved namespace is then used as a prefix for default and relative topic and service names, while absolute names remain unchanged. Backward compatibility is preserved, so models without a namespace continue to use their existing topic and service naming behavior. This feature provides a consistent approach for handling topic and service names across Gazebo plugins. It also allows multiple robots to share the same SDF model while keeping their communication interfaces separate, making multi-robot simulations much easier to set up and maintain. Namespace support has been added to DiffDrive and extended to other drive plugins and sensors, with several PRs still under review. 2. Automated ROS-Gazebo Bridge Previously, users needed to manually configure the names, message types, and communication directions of their bridges. This becomes repetitive when working with many robots that have similar communication interfaces. The new automated bridge can discover matching topics and services on the ROS 2 and Gazebo sides and create the corresponding bridges. As illustrated below, the process consists of three main steps: discovering available interfaces, matching them based on their names and compatible message types, and creating the required bridges. Automated birdge 1744×400 254 KB The feature is optional and can be enabled using the automated_bridge.enable parameter. It also provides two optional configuration parameters: include_patterns : Select which topics and services should be considered. exclude_patterns : Exclude specific topics and services from automated bridging. For example, the following configuration enables automated bridging for interfaces under /robot1 while excluding camera-related topics: # example ros_gz_bridge: ros__parameters: automated_bridge: enable: true include_patterns: - "/robot1.*" exclude_patterns: - ".*camera.*" The automated bridge continuously checks for new interfaces, allowing it to discover topics and services created after the simulation starts. It also supports using manual and automated bridge configurations together. Within the same bridge instance, manually configured bridges take priority, and automated bridging handles the remaining interfaces. To evaluate the overhead of continuous discovery and matching, I tested the automated bridge with a simulation containing 12 robots, 124 Gazebo topics, and 94 Gazebo services, along with a separate ROS 2 node providing 115 topics and 44 services. With actual bridge creation disabled during this test, average CPU usage increased from 2.44% to 3.32% , while memory usage remained nearly unchanged. This suggests that the discovery and matching process adds relatively little overhead in the tested setup. 3. Documentation and Demos Three documentation updates and two demos were prepared to demonstrate the new features and help users get started. Documentation: Model Namespace — How to configure and use model namespaces. Automated Bridge — How to enable and configure automated bridging. Multi-Robot Tutorial — How to use both features together in multi-robot simulations. Demos: Multi-Robot Demo — Demonstrates model namespaces and automated bridging with multiple robots. Warehouse Demo — Demonstrates independent control of four Mecanum-wheel robots sharing the same SDF model. selectedItems.summary: Google DeepMind and UK government work together to reduce planning assessment times
selectedItems.articleText: October 31, 2026 Responsibility & Safety Speeding up planning decisions with AI Owen Larter and David Thacker Share PlanAssist has shown it can cut the time planning officers spend assessing householder applications by up to 58%. PlanAssist - an AI planning tool that handles the heavy lifting of routine applications so officers can focus their expertise where it matters most - is to be made available to an additional 12 local planning authorities across England. In early pilot testing across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset, PlanAssist showed it could bring the average time a planning officer spent on householder assessment tasks down by 58%. Designed to support human judgement, the tool speeds up routine checks while ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every application. Planning bottlenecks have real costs. For the economy, they slow progress toward the UK government's goal of building 1.5 million new homes by 2029. For families, that can mean months of waiting on approval for something as simple as a loft conversion, conservatory, or extension. Built with Gemini, PlanAssist is part of Google DeepMind’s broader partnership with the UK government to explore how AI can help transform planning and other public services. How PlanAssist supports officers Routine householder applications account for up to 70% of planning officers’ workloads. They're often simple to approve but take up a disproportionate share of their time. Developed by Google DeepMind in collaboration with the UK government, Google Cloud, and Faculty, PlanAssist streamlines this work, giving planning officers automated support with processing applications and drafting assessment recommendations. First, it validates application documents and architectural drawings, checking that the required information has been submitted so the application can proceed. Next, it checks the application against heritage constraints (such as tree preservation orders), and local and national planning policies. It also checks whether any issues or objections have previously been raised, such as by local residents. Finally, it drafts fully cited reports that can be edited by planning officers before they reach a final decision. Since June, the tool has been piloted across Barnet, Camden, and Dorset councils, and has shown encouraging early results. In addition to more than halving the officer assessment time per application, more than 70% of the reports generated by the tool - including things like whether an application complies with local planning rules, or whether the applicant has submitted all required documentation - were approved by officers with no edits required. Your browser does not support the video tag. See how Plan Assist works. Moving from pilot to scale PlanAssist is now moving into a 12-month Beta phase using live applications, starting with a subset of councils. Twelve more councils will be onboarded in three cohorts, bringing the total involved to 15. Together, these councils include metropolitan and rural districts across the country, allowing us to test PlanAssist’s capabilities across a diverse range of communities. Subject to successful testing, the government plans for the tool to be made available to all councils in England in 2027, with every assessment reviewed and approved by a qualified planning officer before any decision is made. AI in service of communities Planning decisions shape everyday lives, from a family adding a nursery to a homeowner preparing for winter. By handling time-consuming administrative tasks, and ensuring planning officers retain the final say on every decision, PlanAssist shows how AI can help cut backlogs and approve applications faster. Providing access to these new councils is the natural next step, and we look forward to continuing to support the UK government as they seek to build more homes and unlock economic growth across the country. selectedItems.title: The SEC Should Block Anthropic's IPO to Protect the Public
selectedItems.articleText: Perspective The SEC Should Block Anthropic’s IPO to Protect the Public Matt Scherer / Nov 2, 2026 Matt Scherer is co-author of the recent report Brace for Impact: Protecting people and the economy when the AI bubble bursts . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei looks on as United States President Donald Trump holds a press briefing with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House on September 29, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) Republish Share Things are seldom what they seem when it comes to the finances of the AI industry. The AI ecosystem’s circular business dealings , extensive use of financial engineering , and otherwise murky finances make it hard for investors, regulators, or workers saving for retirement to get an accurate financial picture of AI companies. That is particularly true of Anthropic, which filed the registration statement for its initial public offering (IPO) last week ahead of a planned November stock market debut. The company’s topline financial figures look quite impressive for a startup, with revenues that appear to have grown quickly over the course of 2026 and a fairly healthy balance sheet — on the surface, that is. Dig a little deeper, however, and a far bleaker picture emerges. Footnotes to the company’s most recent financial disclosures revealed nearly $900 billion in spending commitments, most of them stretching into the 2030s. The company’s financial results for 2026 have not been subjected to formal auditing, which makes them less-than-reliable, but the third-quarter results suggest that the company’s revenue growth slowed to a crawl over the summer. Anthropic will have to reverse that trend and sustain extraordinary revenue growth to meet its vast obligations. But the financial pressures that are squeezing Anthropic — and, indeed, the AI industry as a whole — will make it exceptionally hard for the leading model developer to do so. If the company goes public, workers, retail investors, and retirees will increasingly be left holding the bag when Anthropic’s bills come due. The financial mountain that Anthropic must climb is unprecedented for a company making its stock market debut. While Anthropic has an impressive $96 billion in cash reserves, its amended registration statement reveals at least $582 billion in non-cancelable spending commitments to just five companies (Amazon, AMD, Broadcom, Google, and Microsoft) to gain access to the vast computational power required to train and run Anthropic’s generative AI models. Even though they do not appear on Anthropic’s balance sheet, those obligations are effectively debts in a legal and practical sense : they are payments that Anthropic is contractually required to make in the future, regardless of whether the company can afford to do so. Moreover, it is not clear how much of the remaining $300 billion or so of the $895 billion in contractual commitments will ultimately land on Anthropic’s balance sheet. With the company continuing to negotiate further massive infrastructure and compute contracts , Anthropic may well end the year with a trillion dollars or more in contractual commitments. Generating the revenues necessary to meet those obligations would be, to say the least, quite difficult for any company. But the margins of AI model developers are being squeezed by several forces that will make that task extraordinarily challenging for Anthropic. Key forces squeezing the AI industry’s margins AI industry margins Demand pressure: Businesses and consumers may not be willing to pay enough for generative AI. Commoditization: Fierce competition will make it difficult to raise prices. Cost pressures: High costs mean developers can’t cut prices without hemorrhaging cash. External constraints: Supply-chain challenges and community opposition drive up costs and delay revenue generation. Source: Matthew U. Scherer and Maya Jenkins, “Brace for Impact: Protecting People and the Economy When the AI Bubble Bursts,” Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund, October 2026 (Figure 13, p. 30).Interactive graphic: Tech Policy Press First, it isn’t clear that there is nearly enough demand for generative AI products and services to justify Anthropic’s spending. Multiple studies , including from organizations notable for their bullishness on AI, suggest LLMs are not accelerating productivity or otherwise generating positive returns on investment for most businesses . Worryingly for enterprise-focused Anthropic, one study found that the number of Americans using AI at work fell significantly between the summers of 2025 (46%) and 2026 (33%). Anthropic’s spending commitments suggest that the company believes it will be able to convince businesses to pay for ever-larger and more expensive models. But there are growing signs that most businesses are not interested in paying for more powerful and expensive models. When Anthropic released its much-hyped Fable 5 frontier model this summer, its commercial reception was tepid . Our content delivered to your inbox. Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy Thank you! You have successfully joined our subscriber list. Even if a future Anthropic model captivates businesses, the company would run into a second obstacle: the AI industry’s frenzied competition. Anthropic is part of a crowded Silicon Valley ecosystem where numerous well-heeled corporations (including Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and SpaceX, along with Anthropic) offer generative AI models that are largely indistinguishable in their quality and capabilities. As a result, AI companies can quickly offer competing products whenever a rival identifies a use case that shows even a hint of commercial potential. In such an environment, companies can rarely afford to raise prices because doing so will prompt customers simply to switch to a rival. The rush to grab customers ahead of their IPOs led Anthropic and OpenAI to launch a price war this summer that remains ongoing. Competition from Chinese companies offering open-weights models puts further downward pressure on prices, as does the increasing availability of models that can run locally on phones and laptops — no expensive data centers required. That leads to the third problem: the extraordinarily high costs of the chips and data centers needed to train and run AI models, which put powerful and continuous upward pressure on Anthropic’s costs. Between the chips, servers, networking equipment, electricity and cooling infrastructure, construction costs, and other expenses, a 1 gigawatt (GW) data center costs an estimated $31 billion , and the prices for some components are soaring. That is for 1 GW. Anthropic has committed to 15 GW of data center capacity in the coming years and the company estimates it will ultimately need 20-25 GW, which explains the company’s half-trillion-plus dollars in spending commitments. And that is just the cost of the physical infrastructure. Once a data center is up and running, training AI models entails using tens of thousands of chips running in parallel that require massive amounts of energy to power, run hot, and need to be kept cool. Moreover, each time someone prompts a model to answer a question, create an image, or perform a task, additional computational power, energy, and cooling are needed to process the query and generate a response or complete the task. Finally, there are external factors that are delaying data center construction and piling on additional costs. The fierce and still-rising backlash to AI in general and data centers in particular across the country has scuttled a number of data center projects and delayed many others. Every delay limits the computational capacity Anthropic is counting on to generate the revenue it will desperately need, and rising costs due to the Iran War and supply-chain challenges could drive Anthropic’s operational costs still higher. Anthropic will further pad its cash reserves if its IPO is successful, but the brutal economics of its business are not likely to improve anytime soon. Even if demand picks up significantly, intense competition will apply unrelenting downward pressure on prices even as high costs and resource constraints squeeze it from the opposite direction. That is a deadly mix for Anthropic in light of its slowing revenue growth and massive off-balance-sheet debts, a vast and immovable fixed cost. If Anthropic were to go public now, it would pile additional risk onto a stock market that is already historically overvalued and disproportionately concentrated in a handful of tightly interconnected mega-cap companies from the tech sector. That has already created a risk of a historically damaging stock market crash ; never before has such a huge amount of wealth depended on the performance of a small number of companies whose fortunes are inextricably linked. Adding another huge, unprofitable tech giant to public exchanges would exacerbate both of those factors and create a higher risk of contagion if (or, rather, when) Anthropic reaches a financial precipice. It also would mean that an ever-larger share of the fallout from a potentially devastating AI crash would fall on ordinary people. As a private company, Anthropic’s shares are overwhelmingly owned by corporate insiders, tech giants, and venture capitalists. Once the company goes public and shares start getting funneled into 401(k)s, retirement accounts, and index funds, it will be workers, retirees, and retail investors that are increasingly left holding the bag when the forces squeezing Anthropic’s margins start to bite. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has the power to stop that from happening. The agency can delay or stop companies from going public if it believes a company’s registration statement is “on its face incomplete or inaccurate in any material respect .” That legislative language might as well have been written with Anthropic in mind, considering that the company’s prospectus includes only unaudited financial results for the period where it claims the greatest revenue growth, relegates its most significant future obligations to the footnotes of its registration statement, and has continued to announce new 11-digit financial commitments as its IPO approaches. The SEC should block Anthropic’s stock market debut until the company provides two consecutive quarters of audited financial statements, with all material information about the company’s spending commitments disclosed. Failing to do so could have dire consequences for workers, investors, and ultimately the financial system and economy. Source: Agility Robotics Agility Robotics has cleared a major hurdle in its planned initial public offering (IPO). Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the special purpose acquisition company’s (SPAC) proposed business combination with the humanoid developer, moving Agility closer to becoming a publicly-traded company. More than 84% of votes cast at a special shareholder meeting on Nov. 2 supported the deal. The SPAC is expected to close on Nov. 4. The combined company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker symbol AGLT. Churchill Capital stock finished up nearly 14% on Nov. 2. The transaction is expected to provide Agility with approximately $465 million in gross capital before expenses. That funding will support commercial expansion, customer deployments and manufacturing capacity as the company looks to scale its Digit humanoid robot business. The revised capital figure reflects a reduction from the more than $620 million in gross proceeds anticipated when the merger was announced in June. Following the expiration of Churchill XI’s shareholder redemption deadline, the companies now expect approximately $164 million from Churchill’s trust account, approximately $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) financing led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity funding Agility received following the initial SPAC announcement. The original transaction valued Agility at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value. Existing Agility shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company rather than receive cash in the transaction. Agility is entering the public markets with more than a proposed product roadmap. Its Digit robots are already operating in 9 customer environments, with logistics and manufacturing emerging as the company’s primary commercial markets. One of its most established relationships is with GXO Logistics. The companies began working together in 2023 and signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service agreement in 2024 to deploy Digit at GXO’s facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. There, Digit has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors. In October, the companies announced an expansion to two additional GXO facilities: Statesville, N.C., and Lebanon, Tenn. Digit will initially support repetitive material-handling tasks in e-commerce fulfillment operations. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 using Digit 4, with plans to transition to the newer Digit 5 as it becomes commercially available. Agility is also moving into manufacturing. In October, agricultural equipment maker AGCO signed a commercial agreement to pilot Digit at its Hesston , Kan., production facility beginning in 2027. Initial tasks will include sorting and stacking parts and placing totes for storage. Submit your innovation now! The company says early access for customers is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of that year. That order figure is an important indicator of customer interest, but it should not be confused with current revenue. The multi-year value is expected to be realized over time and remains subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications. Agility’s RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Ore., is designed for annual production capacity of up to 10,000 robots. The company is also expanding its software, deployment and service capabilities, including through its Agility Arc fleet-management platform. Credit: Eugene Demaitre Real-world data, human “tutors,” and simulation are all part of the recipe for training AI models to enable next-generation robots to tackle a widening variety of tasks. Tutor Intelligence Inc. today said it has raised $75 million in Series B funding as it works toward general-purpose robotics. “It’s not only that Tutor’s models let robots do jobs that robots have never been able to do before,” stated Josh Gruenstein, co-founder and CEO of Tutor Intelligence. “This type of intelligence also makes robots affordable on a whole new level. We’re unlocking much broader access to the solutions that businesses need to survive and that make basic goods cheaper for everybody. And the demand is there. We can hardly build robots fast enough.” Tutor Intelligence spun out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (MIT CSAIL ) in 2021. The Watertown, Mass.-based company asserted that it is building a full technology stack to “close the gap between what robots can do and what people can do.” Data flywheel accelerates robot deployment “Artificial intelligence has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images,” said Tutor Intelligence. “The physical world has no such record to train on, and AI has yet to transform it in the same way.” The company has deployed fleets of internet-connected robots into production environments, where they do real work for customers with input from remote operators known as “tutors.” It uses the real-world data to train better frontier models, ultimately making the robots more capable. Tutor claimed that its “full-stack platform” and “data flywheel” accelerate deployment, making robots more scalable, safer, and more affordable. Instead of a robots-as-a-service (RaaS ) model, business pay Tutor by the hour or by the pick, the same way they pay for manual labor. Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, added Tutor. The company said it handles deployment and maintenance and regularly sends software and intelligence upgrades. Tutor said its approach is bringing automation to tasks that have long defied conventional, deterministic robotics. It opened a “Data Factory ” earlier this year to evaluate policies across 100 physical robots. Submit your innovation now! Tutor Intelligence gets traction with Sonny and Cassie Tutor’s Data Factory includes the Sonny two-armed, semi-humanoid robots for each picking. Cassie is a mobile manipulator designed for case picking and palletizing . The company reported that twice as many of its robots are working in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago. The robots are currently moving, lifting, and manipulating objects across some of the country’s largest manufacturing and logistics networks.
